title: Sleep, Insomnia & the Psychology of Rest
description: First unit: Sleep pressure accumulated through waking. Work through real situations, competing explanations and practical choices.

lessons.title: What is really happening?
lessons.teach: Bea finished a night shift and feels exhausted at 10 am, but has been struggling to fall asleep when she gets home.

nodes.title: Watch the conversation
nodes.prompt: Listen closely to what each person says and what still remains uncertain.
nodes.explanation: Time awake builds homeostatic sleep pressure, while circadian timing changes biological readiness for sleep. These processes can point in different directions after shift work.
nodes.counterexample: Feeling exhausted does not guarantee immediate sleep, and inability to sleep at a particular time does not demonstrate that sleep pressure is absent.
nodes.sources: Borbély (1982), two-process model; NICE guidance on insomnia and shift-work-related sleep difficulties.
nodes.scenario: Bea finished a night shift and feels exhausted at 10 am, but has been struggling to fall asleep when she gets home.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I've been awake for sixteen hours. I should fall asleep immediately.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Do you usually find it easy to sleep when the sun is up?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: No. I feel worn out, but my brain seems unusually alert at this time.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: What was your sleep schedule before night shifts?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I normally wake around seven in the morning.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: So you're trying to sleep when your body clock is used to waking?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: That could explain why tiredness alone isn't doing the job.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Sleep pressure and your body clock may be pulling in different directions.

options.feedback: Direct self-report helps, but a tentative formulation can still be tested against observed circumstances.

nodes.explanation: Investigate a difference that the rival explanations predict. Record habitual sleep times, shift schedule and light/caffeine exposure rather than judging only by tiredness.

lessons.title: Try it in another situation
lessons.teach: Apply the way of reasoning to a different situation. Do not import the first case’s verdict.

nodes.title: A new situation
nodes.body:
A traveller feels exhausted after flying overnight yet lies awake in their hotel at the destination's usual bedtime, which is midday according to their previous body clock.

Decide what you can infer from this example without assuming the same explanation must apply.

options.label: Treat the visible similarity as a reliable indication that the behaviour has the same psychological function.
options.feedback: Similar behaviours can protect very different interests depending on the context.

options.label: Consider what the person could be trying to gain or avoid, then test that explanation against the circumstances and credible alternatives.

options.label: Postpone all interpretation until the person can give an account of their private motives.
options.feedback: A perfect self-report may be unavailable. Tentative, revisable inferences can still be useful.

options.label: Judge whether the behaviour is socially acceptable first, since that provides the best evidence about why it happened.
options.feedback: Judging the consequences of a behaviour is important, but consequences do not by themselves establish motive.

nodes.explanation: The words are evidence. Both the preferred explanation and its rival are interpretations requiring further testing. Feeling exhausted does not guarantee immediate sleep, and inability to sleep at a particular time does not demonstrate that sleep pressure is absent.

nodes.title: An idea worth carrying forward
nodes.body:
Time awake builds homeostatic sleep pressure, while circadian timing changes biological readiness for sleep. These processes can point in different directions after shift work.

Feeling exhausted does not guarantee immediate sleep, and inability to sleep at a particular time does not demonstrate that sleep pressure is absent.

The purpose of the exercise is to make a better-supported judgement and choose a proportionate next step.
nodes.sources: Borbély (1982), two-process model; NICE guidance on insomnia and shift-work-related sleep difficulties.
